items.title: What next for the Democrats? | Martin Wolf on the US midterms | FT
items.author: Financial Times
items.content:
<article>Americans roundly rejected the Republican Party under President Donald Trump at the ballot box, giving the Democratic Party control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate.

items.title: Why Is Everyone Leaving New Zealand?
items.author: Bloomberg Originals
items.content:
<article>While much of the world thinks of New Zealand as an idyllic redoubt far removed from the world’s problems, one to which many a billionaire has decamped, its working-age population is leaving in record numbers. And many of those emigrating are in their 30s and 40s – professionals with friends and family – rather than college graduates who often return a few years later. 

In this Bloomberg Originals mini-documentary, we explore how successive New Zealand governments have built the world’s most extreme housing market, and how in doing so set the stage for the current exodus. Has stagnant growth and a cost-of-living crisis ended the Kiwi dream – and if so, what can be done to fix it?

Explore these and other related stories in more depth on Bloomberg.com

https://youtu.be/gAQ6t3F_2Ug

DESCRIPTION
Artie Shevchenko, a former Google engineer who is now at Canva and teaches at ITMO University, tells Titus Winters how his book “Code Health Guardian” came together: the internal code review classes he built at Google (over 1,000 Googlers attended, with a 4.5-star rating), a talk on A Philosophy of Software Design, and years of teaching a university course. He keeps that book's three complexity problems (change amplification, cognitive load, and unknown unknowns), which he says help you rank what to fix first. But he doesn't agree with its two causes, obscurity and dependencies. Dependencies are also the building blocks of all software, so he replaces them with six more specific causes: untrue interfaces, complex interfaces, unfamiliarity, too many dependencies, duplication, and unstable dependencies. Titus agrees that "all dependencies are bad" misses the point, since every dependency is both a benefit and a liability.

The AI conversation turns on understanding. Artie compares models to two types of exam students who give nearly identical answers: one who understands the material and one who memorized it. Most of the time you can get away with the second kind, but not always, so a human "code health guardian" still has to validate AI output or risk losing intellectual control of the codebase. He admits he's still learning how to prioritize reviews, and no longer reads every test line as carefully. Titus adds that his top worry is whatever is hardest to change later (dependencies, frameworks, state storage, API design, database schemas), which lines up with Artie's view that interfaces sit at the top of the list. They also discuss intellectual versus statistical control (tests as evidence), and Artie makes the case for "semi-functional programming," meaning immutability by default, which reduces obscurity. Titus ties it to testing: stateless code is trivial to test, and mutable state is where time enters the problem. Both stress that nobody has the full playbook for AI-assisted development yet.

items.title: From hate to peace - The power of reconciliation | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Against hate and exclusion; for respect and tolerance. Initiatives in Germany, the U.S. and Colombia show how reconciliation can work - between religions, political opponents, victims and perpetrators.

Colombian Kelly Diaz was just a child when terrorists shot and killed her father. Now, 22 years on, she's meeting his killer in prison. She wants to forgive him and finally make peace with it all. For years now, a unique reconciliation project has been helping her prepare for that moment. It's an initiative launched by Stuttgart-based social entrepreneur Tobias Merckle. "It's a liberating process for both sides. Victims can leave hatred and thoughts of revenge behind, while perpetrators can take responsibility for their crimes and experience forgiveness," he says. Their journey doesn't end there, though. Both victims and perpetrators will go on to work together rebuilding places destroyed by civil war - what are known as "villages of reconciliation." 

Concern is also mounting over increasing political polarization in the United States. Republicans versus Democrats, right against left - the rifts in society seem to be deepening. The Braver Angels initiative is using dialogue as an attempt to turn that trend around. Since 2016, it's been running workshops where participants practice active listening and respectful debate. The goal is constructive exchange across the political divide.
Munich-based YouthBridge has made it its mission to prevent polarization from ever taking hold in the first place. It brings together young people from various backgrounds, from many religions and different walks of life. Jewish and Muslim college students engage in dialogue, alongside other young people from other cultural backgrounds. Can bridges be built to connect different communities? Is hate and exclusion preventable? "Our society is very divided, everyone retreats into their own bubble," says 18-year-old Begüm Tan. "We need to reach out again to one another, even if we don't always agree." YouthBridge trains young people to become multipliers who can develop their own social, cultural and media projects - promoting peaceful coexistence.

items.author: The People Profiles
items.content:
<article>Sir John Hawkwood: a documentary on the Essex-born captain of the White Company, the English condottiere who fought for Milan, the Pope and Florence.

Painted by Paolo Uccello on the wall of Florence Cathedral in 1436, Giovanni Acuto was in fact John Hawkwood, a tanner's son from Essex. After serving as a longbowman in the Hundred Years' War, he crossed into Italy with the White Company in 1361 and spent three decades selling his sword to Pisa, Milan, the Papacy, Padua and Florence. The story takes in the Cesena massacre, his marriage to Donnina Visconti, daughter of Bernabò Visconti, his victory at Castagnaro in 1387 and his death in Florence in 1394.

items.title: North Korea - Propaganda and the next generation | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>North Korea: A small country often at the center of global attention for geopolitical reasons. The Kim dynasty has ruled through oppression and isolation since 1948. Yet the regime is striving to project a new image.

Luxury resorts, an international marathon in the capital and a ruling family portrayed in a surprisingly approachable light: Recently, North Korea has been showing the world a very different face. Is the country, up until now known primarily for repression and isolation, undergoing an image change? This documentary looks behind the scenes and reveals the contradictions of a country caught between cautious openness and unrelenting control.

On one hand, a new apparent openness is emerging through sporting events attended by carefully selected international participants. Images of what looks like a thriving economy are being disseminated beyond the country's borders: Online shopping in Pyongyang, idyllic beaches with modern holiday facilities, and even streaming services for wealthy North Koreans loyal to the regime.

State television shows cheerful locals treating themselves to a break at the seaside resort of Wonsan after toiling hard for the motherland. Around 80 per cent of the population are now said to own a mobile phone - albeit with access restricted to state-approved North Korean apps.

Ruler Kim Jong Un is also embracing the image campaign, with more frequent public appearances alongside his daughter Kim Ju Ae. Is she being groomed to be a potential successor? Or is this family-centered turn intended to give the regime a more human face?

At the same time, the state continues to crack down hard on any form of undesirable behavior. Archival footage and reports from refugee organizations document public trials of young people caught consuming South Korean pop culture. International experts emphasize that a change in the country's public image by no means signifies an end to surveillance, punishment and censorship.

Join us at GOTO Copenhagen 2027, October 4–8. https://gotocph.com/2027?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=cph26-talks

Adam Tornhill - Founder and CTO at CodeScene Programmer, psychologist, Lisp hacker, speaker and author of several books including "Your Code as a Crime Scene" @adamtornhill2546


RESOURCES

ABSTRACT
Have you seen early productivity gains from AI, only to watch them disappear under growing complexity and production incidents? You're not alone. There's a common reason: many production systems already struggle with technical debt. When AI agents enter the development loop, that debt becomes a multiplier. Poor-quality code not only increases defects and costs. It dramatically raises AI risk by driving high breakage rates, turning promising AI agents into legacy code generators rather than genuine help.

Fortunately, there's hope on the horizon. In this talk, Adam Tornhill shows how organizations can achieve both speed and quality with AI. Backed by large-scale empirical studies on AI coding and developer productivity, we separate what works from what doesn't in real-world systems. Building on these findings, we then look at a practical framework for driving and sustaining AI-friendly code at scale. The AI revolution is here. Is your code ready?

items.title: Why the right can't stop talking about communism
items.author: Vox
items.content:
<article>There’s been a lot of “communist” talk on the midterms campaign trail. It’s become Trump’s favorite new perceived threat coming from the left. But it’s actually not new at all. 

US politicians, especially on the right, have long described communism as a threat to the American way of life. As a result, the United States has undergone historical periods of intense and occasionally violent means to suppress the spread of communism. Beyond the clash between capitalism and communism as economic systems, a line is often drawn between communist ideology and religion in America, specifically Christianity. 

In the 1950s, President Dwight D. Eisenhower added the words “Under God” to the Pledge of Allegiance, doubling down on the Christian values of an anti-communist America. The phrase “In God We Trust” was also added to US currency. As evangelical Christians grew into a crucial voting bloc for the Republican party, communist accusations against the left have appeared now and again to mobilize the base.

Hosted by Kahlil Greene, this video is part of our new series Kahlil Explains that unites Vox’s unique brand of explainer journalism with Greene’s expertise in how politics and culture shape society. This episode traces the history of communism in America and its clash with religious groups to unpack why Democratic candidates are being labeled communists and whether the strategy will resonate with voters today.

Read more about communism and religion in America:

Andrew Hartman’s book Karl Marx in America: https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/K/bo245100866.html

Vox’s Today, Explained covers Trump's imaginary Red Scare: https://www.vox.com/podcasts/498360/trump-democratic-socialists-communism-red-scare

items.title: Grokking the Brain: What AI Reveals About How You Learn • Barbara Oakley • GOTO Copenhagen 2026
items.author: GOTO Conferences
items.content:
<article>This presentation was recorded at GOTO Copenhagen 2026. #GOTOcon #GOTOcph
Join us at GOTO Copenhagen 2027, October 4–8. https://gotocph.com/2027?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=cph26-talks

Barbara Oakley - Professor of Engineering at Oakland University @BarbaraOakley


RESOURCES
https://x.com/Barbara97881398
https://www.linkedin.com/in/barbaraoakley/
https://barbaraoakley.com/
https://gotopia.tech/experts/1554/barbara-oakley


ABSTRACT
Train an AI model long past the point where it has memorized its examples, and something strange happens — it stops memorizing and suddenly "groks" the pattern beneath them. That hard-won pattern can then be "distilled" into a smaller, faster model that runs it with ease. These are ideas from AI — but they may give us our clearest view yet of the human brain. We grok a hard skill slowly, with conscious effort, then distill it into a fast, automatic system that needs no effort at all. That is what expertise is.

The same “machinery” has a quieter side. A model is aligned by its training data — and in an analogous fashion, so are humans. Give me a child to the age of seven, the old saying goes, and I'll show you the adult. But adults are aligned too, usually without knowing it — and a brain aligned a little too well can harden into a mental fortress, deflecting new ideas.

Curiosity provides a way out. Dopamine—reward-based learning—fuels the brain's ability to rewire — it helps us build new links, keeps the fortress gate open, and keeps hard-won knowledge from setting into a wall. We'll look at what all this means for how you learn, how you use AI, and how you keep thinking for yourself in an age that makes it easy not to.

RESOURCES

ABSTRACT
Oh great, another session about AI. Your social media feeds are already flooded with agentic this and spec-driven that; one-shot rewrites and everyone-is-a-programmer-now.

I am not using genAI to go faster but to go broader. It lets me offload (significant) side concerns in areas where I am competent but have no wish to become proficient; the time-sink supporting work that I would either hack together badly myself or side-step altogether.

I want to share some models and metaphors that are helping me make sense of this new world: why Ward Cunningham hates printers; how riding a fixie isn’t really cycling; why I'm treating Claude as a fantastic researcher and a terrible programmer; how test-first is the new TDD.

I am calling this adjacent engineering. Sometimes these side quests become significant enough to spin off into their own entire product, which I call adjacent discovery.

My goal is to give you a more nuanced take on generative AI, to help you cut through all the noise and get actual work done.

items.title: Inside the Deadly 1993 Firefight in Somalia | Ambush in Mogadishu (full documentary) | FRONTLINE
items.author: FRONTLINE PBS | Official
items.content:
<article>The inside story of a tragic 1993 battle in Mogadishu, Somalia, that left 18 Americans and hundreds of Somalis dead. At the time, it was known as the most violent U.S. combat firefight since Vietnam. The battle of Mogadishu went on to inspire the movie “Black Hawk Down.” (Aired 1998)

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb

And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate
On Oct. 3, 1993, a planned 90-minute U.S. mission to capture Somali warlord Mohammed Farah Aidid in Mogadishu turned into a deadly 17-hour urban firefight in which hundreds of people died. Armed with automatic weapons and rocket-propelled grenades, Somali fighters shot down two U.S. military helicopters and ambushed elite U.S. Army Rangers and Delta Force units. The Clinton administration would announce plans to withdraw U.S. forces from Somalia days later.

The 1998 documentary “Ambush in Mogadishu” investigates what led up to the disaster — including a civil war and famine in Somalia, attacks on U.N. peacekeepers by Aidid’s forces, muddled U.S. military and diplomatic policy on Somalia, and Washington, D.C.’s failure to coordinate with the U.S. military on the ground.

In forensic detail, “Ambush in Mogadishu” goes inside the firefight that trapped a number of U.S. Army Rangers as they moved into a maze of alleys in Mogadishu to try to save comrades on a downed Black Hawk helicopter. In the documentary, surviving Rangers paint extraordinarily vivid pictures of an intense and bloody battle that took a deadly toll on U.S. forces and also killed an estimated 350-1,000 Somalis, including civilians.

The battle of Mogadishu went on to cast a long shadow on U.S. military decision-making about humanitarian and peacekeeping operations. Part of the tragedy’s legacy, experts said in the documentary, was a U.S. reluctance to be drawn into crises in the ‘90s in other volatile countries, such as Bosnia, Rwanda and Haiti. 

“Ambush in Mogadishu” was a FRONTLINE co-production with InVision Productions, Ltd. in association with BBC-2. The writer, producer and director was William Cran. The executive producer was Michael Sullivan. The senior executive producer was David Fanning.
Explore additional reporting on “Ambush in Mogadishu”:

ABSTRACT
Have you seen early productivity gains from AI, only to watch them disappear under growing complexity and production incidents? You're not alone. There's a common reason: many production systems already struggle with technical debt. When AI agents enter the development loop, that debt becomes a multiplier. Poor-quality code not only increases defects and costs. It dramatically raises AI risk by driving high breakage rates, turning promising AI agents into legacy code generators rather than genuine help.

Fortunately, there's hope on the horizon. In this talk, Adam Tornhill shows how organizations can achieve both speed and quality with AI. Backed by large-scale empirical studies on AI coding and developer productivity, we separate what works from what doesn't in real-world systems. Building on these findings, we then look at a practical framework for driving and sustaining AI-friendly code at scale. The AI revolution is here. Is your code ready?

items.title: Decoding conflicts - Sudan: The forgotten war | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Tens of thousands have died in Sudan's war, and millions have been displaced. Why is the world's largest humanitarian crisis receiving so little attention?

War has raged in Sudan since April 2023, when the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces began fighting the Sudanese army. Civilians have paid the price for this power struggle. The situation in Darfur is particularly dire, where experts and the United Nations have long warned of signs of genocide.

Why is this war receiving so little international attention? What impact will cuts to international aid have on a country facing such an immense humanitarian crisis? And what role are outside powers such as the United Arab Emirates, Egypt, Russia and the United States playing in the conflict? What interests drive these governments to support one side or the other with weapons and funding?

Accounts from those affected reveal the devastating impact of the war on the people of Sudan. A journalist from El Fasher, forced to flee the city, discovers videos of murdered family members and friends circulating on social media. A young doctor spent years performing surgery in trenches or amid bombardment. Experts had warned of a looming humanitarian catastrophe for years. Yet the crisis has continued to escalate. Meanwhile, young Sudanese people are fighting to draw the world's attention to what is happening in their country. This film traces the origins of the conflict, who is fueling it, and what responsibility Europe shares.

items.title: The World's Most Aggressive EV Push Isn't in China | Bloomberg Primer
items.author: Bloomberg Originals
items.content:
<article>(Corrects the spelling of Mia Mottley at 06:01) In 2024, Ethiopia became the first country to ban imports of new gasoline-powered cars, and the main reason wasn't global warming. Ethiopia was spending billions of dollars every year on imported fuel it couldn’t afford, and subsequently defaulted on its debt. Cheap hydropower from Africa’s largest dam made electric vehicles a practical alternative, and Chinese-made EVs — some assembled locally — quickly filled dealership lots. Today, Ethiopia’s EV share outpaces the global average. But sticker prices are too high for most, the grid remains patchy and armed conflict is flaring in the country and across the region. Can Ethiopia make its unprecedented bet on EVs pay off?

items.title: How Silicon Valley conquered the business of war | The Gray Area
items.author: Vox
items.content:
<article>Silicon Valley says it can build better weapons, faster and cheaper than traditional defense contractors. But what happens when the companies making those weapons also get a say in how they’re used?

Subscribe to our channel! http://goo.gl/0bsAjO

In today’s episode, Vox reporter and producer Miles Bryan talks with long-time national security journalist Sharon Weinberger, author of Valley of Death: How Big Tech Is Fueling the Future of War. The book traces Silicon Valley’s deep ties to the military and its return to the weapons business through companies like Palantir, SpaceX, and Anduril. Sharon says this raises troubling questions of how private funding gives tech founders greater control over military technology, and whether their promises of innovation justify risks to accountability.

In this episode, Miles and Sharon explore the surprising CIA contract that helped keep Steve Jobs’s company afloat, how “tech companies” sell their visions to the Pentagon, if their innovations live up to the hype, and whether tech’s disruption of the defense industry could leave us with a more powerful version of the same old system.

items.title: No future in Germany? Why skilled Polish workers are going home | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Ever more Poles are leaving Germany, while fewer and fewer are moving the other way. Why do they no longer see a future for themselves in Germany? What's drawing them back to Poland? And what does it all mean for German companies?

Philip Panek chose his university with a goal in mind: the European University Viadrina in Frankfurt on the Oder, right on the German-Polish border. When he began his studies, he planned to stay in Germany and build a career there. Now, he's planning to complete his legal traineeship in Poland. There, he says, he has more than just family and friends waiting for him — he also sees new economic opportunities.

Michael Sünkler can also see that Germany is losing its appeal for many Polish workers. The managing director of a transportation company has many employees from Poland. In recent years, however, many have left. For him, the departure of skilled Polish workers is not an abstract political issue — it's a tangible economic problem. One of those employees is Tomasz. The truck driver has worked in Berlin for over ten years, but rising living costs are taking their toll. Rent and groceries have become significantly more expensive, he says. As soon as his daughter finishes school, he plans to return to Poland with his family.

Kamila Gierko and her husband, Zbyszek Perzyna, have already done just that. Six months ago, they moved from Berlin to Szczecin. For years, Germany offered them favorable conditions for self-employment. But bureaucracy and a lack of digital services, along with high taxes and social contributions were increasingly weighing them down. Their experiences in Poland have been very different: More administrative processes are digital, and the tax burden is lower. Germany, they say, has lost its momentum.

This report follows people whose real-life decisions reveal more than statistics can. It profiles a law student who wants to start a career and a family in Poland, an entrepreneur fighting to retain every Polish employee he can, a truck driver reassessing the cost-benefit analysis of his life, and a couple who have already moved back to their home country.

items.title: Mary Shelley - The Dark Birth of Frankenstein Documentary
items.author: The People Profiles
items.content:
<article>Mary Shelley documentary: the tragic life behind Frankenstein, from her elopement with Percy Bysshe Shelley to Lord Byron's ghost story contest at Lake Geneva.

Mary Shelley was born in London in 1797 to the philosopher William Godwin and the feminist Mary Wollstonecraft, who died days later. At 16 she eloped with the married poet Percy Bysshe Shelley, and in the wet summer of 1816 a ghost story challenge set by Lord Byron gave her the idea for Frankenstein, published anonymously in 1818. Grief followed her: the suicides of her half-sister Fanny and Percy's first wife Harriet, the deaths of three of her four children and Percy's drowning in 1822. Widowed at 24, she lived by her pen, writing The Last Man and editing her husband's poems until her death in 1851.

items.title: Cargo sailboats: A sea change for shipping? | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>The shipping industry is facing radical change, with a goal of becoming climate-neutral by 2050. Are cargo sailboats — which harness wind power using yacht-racing technology and digital weather routing — the solution?

The shipping industry is under pressure. It's responsible for about three percent of global CO₂ emissions and is expected to become climate-neutral by 2050. To achieve this aim, wind power is coming under the spotlight. A remarkable experiment is underway on the world's oceans, to find out how to make the best possible use of wind energy. Largely unnoticed by the public, the first modern cargo sailing ship was launched in France in 2020. The voyage was deemed a success.

Also in France, the 81-meter "Anemos" — currently the world's largest sail-powered cargo ship — set sail in 2024. The inter-island freighter "Juren AE," which operates in the Marshall Islands, was developed by the University of Applied Sciences Emden/Leer. It too demonstrates the feasibility of emission-free shipping.

In technical terms, these ships are modeled after the high-tech racing yachts used by professional sailors such as Isabelle Joschke and Boris Herrmann. Carbon masts, optimized hulls and digital weather routing enable fast, safe and efficient voyages. These innovations are setting the standard — just like in the automotive industry, where motor racing technologies are incorporated into vehicles on the production line. Cargo sailboats are now demonstrating that if shipping is to become climate-neutral, wind power is crucial.

items.title: Inside Mexico City’s Housing Theft Crisis
items.author: Bloomberg Originals
items.content:
<article>In Mexico City, housing theft happens on average 11 times a day, often when homeowners are on vacation or have died, leaving properties vacant. In many cases criminal gangs move in, claiming ownership in an effort to profit from a gentrification wave that’s boosted home prices.

Many such “dispossessions” can involve title fraud and even complicit public officials. Mexico City recorded 2,676 cases this year through August, according to public records, bringing the total over the past decade to nearly 41,000. 

The sheer number of incidents lays bare two key problems for President Claudia Sheinbaum: security and the cost of living. While homicides have plunged under her watch, reports of extortion are at their highest in more than a decade. She also has made expanding access to affordable homes a national priority, yet nowhere is the challenge more stark than the capital, where protests frequently break out over evictions and rising foreign demand.

items.title: Between Capitol Hill and Black Broadway - Washington, D.C.'s hidden worlds | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Barely a day goes by without images of Washington, D.C. being  in the media. The US capital is the nation's political heart, and its iconic landmarks exude a sense of history.

Washington's monuments and memorials are known around the world. They tell the story of the United States, from the White House to the Capitol and the Lincoln Memorial, where Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his famous "I Have a Dream" speech.

But proximity to the corridors of power is just one reason for the city's appeal. Away from the monumental avenues and boulevards lies a vibrant cultural scene that dances to the beat of go-go. The genre, created by local African American musicians, still fills the funk clubs on what's known as "Black Broadway" in the U Street neighborhood.

Washington is a city of contrasts. In the 1970s, its nonwhite majority population gave it the nickname "Chocolate City." It's a place where people of all kinds try to realize humanity's greatest ideas: freedom, equality, democracy and human rights. D.C. is a political idea, carved in the marble of its monuments. And yet behind its famous facades, the city has more to offer than many realize.

items.title: How Do Fungi Keep the Planet Healthy? | PODCAST: The Joy of Why
items.author: Quanta Magazine
items.content:
<article>Evolutionary biologist Toby Kiers explains how fungal networks in soil trade nutrients with plants, help keep carbon underground, and strike bargains without having a brain.

“The Joy of Why” is a Quanta Magazine podcast about curiosity and the pursuit of knowledge. The mathematician and author Steven Strogatz and the cosmologist and author Janna Levin take turns interviewing leading researchers about the great scientific and mathematical questions of our time.  For more episodes visit Quanta Magazine: https://www.quantamagazine.org/tag/the-joy-of-why/

---------

0:00 Introduction
2:42 What Are Mycorrhizal Fungi?
5:30 How Plants and Fungi Trade Resources
8:00 Inside the Underground Fungal Network
11:30 How Fungi Shape Climate and Ecosystems
16:05 The Underground Marketplace: Cooperation and Competition
26:15 How Fungi Make Decisions Without Brains
29:40 The Hidden Partnership Between Fungi and Bacteria
34:14 Watching Nutrients Move Through Fungal Networks
40:28 Mapping and Protecting Earth's Underground Biodiversity
45:00 The Strange Biology of Fungi
49:35 What Fungi Reveal About Cooperation in Nature

---------

People may think of soil as just dirt, but it is anything but inert. Beneath your feet, a vast network of mycorrhizal fungi is hard at work, trading minerals with plant roots. This trading system helps enrich the soil, and it sequesters 13 billion tons of atmospheric carbon dioxide each year — roughly equivalent to one-third of the world’s fossil-fuel emissions. Scientists know that these fungi form partnerships with 80% of all plant species on Earth, a relationship that evolved some 450 million years ago. What they have not understood is how organisms with no brain or central nervous system can decide whom to trade with, and on what terms.

Toby Kiers, an evolutionary biologist at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, has spent much of her career making this hidden world visible. Drawing on economics and game theory, and using tools that range from fluorescent quantum dots to imaging robots, her lab is probing how fungi and plants conduct their trade. The work raises new questions about soil, carbon, and even what counts as an individual organism. In this episode, Kiers tells co-host Steven Strogatz how these brainless, decentralized organisms can behave strategically — discriminating between better and worse partners and shifting resources across the network to wherever a plant will “pay” more for it — and how she has built a worldwide community of researchers

In this episode, Vox host Jonquilyn Hill talks with Idrees Kahloon, staff writer at the Atlantic, about why he believes America has become a gerontocracy – a government whose rulers are older than the rest of the population. There’s the age of political leaders in Congress and the White House. And there’s also the economic impact of having Americans over the age of 55 holding nearly three-quarters of the nation's wealth.

Jonquilyn and Idrees examine how this demographic and economic shift came to pass over the last several decades. They get into the political taboo over reforming Social Security and Medicare, the impact of housing market restrictions and zoning on younger home buyers, and the ways that government spending heavily favors older voters.

items.title: The King Obsessed With Witches
items.author: History Hit
items.content:
<article>Maddy Pelling and Anthony Delaney investigate one of Europe’s bloodiest witch hunts: Scotland’s North Berwick Witch trials of 1591. In this extraordinary case, fears escalated all the way up the social hierarchy to the King himself, James VI. A wild storm in the North Sea had nearly killed James and his new wife Anne of Denmark, fuelling his fascination with the intellectual study of demonology. A maelstrom of terror brought together the King’s paranoia of a conspiracy against him with local rivalries and misfortune, twisting together the fates of individuals from maidservants to magistrates, in the hunt for scapegoats.

Maddy and Anthony meet at Edinburgh’s Holyrood Palace, the place where the King himself interrogated one of the alleged witches, Agnes Sampson, a local healer and midwife. This was a remarkable moment when different worlds met, king and commoner, captured through the accounts of her confession.

But who were the accused, and how were their confessions extracted? Maddy and Anthony travel through this area of Scotland and examine the records to understand how the fear of witches spread through entire communities, and how the women and men of North Berwick were tragically caught up in the terror.

items.author: GOTO Conferences
items.content:
<article>This interview was recorded for the GOTO Book Club. #GOTOcon #GOTObookclub
http://gotopia.tech/bookclub

Check out more here:

Matt Erman - Author of "Grokking Software Architecture" @CodeLiftSleep 
Luca Mezzalira - Solutions Architect, Consultant, International Speaker & Author of "Building Micro-Frontends" @My50c 

RESOURCES

https://x.com/codeliftsleep
https://blogs.realworldbooks.academy
https://www.linkedin.com/company/codeliftsleep

Luca
https://www.buildingmicrofrontends.com
https://twitter.com/lucamezzalira
https://www.linkedin.com/in/lucamezzalira
https://linktr.ee/lucamezzalira
https://lucamezzalira.com

DESCRIPTION
Matt Erman, a senior software engineer at Blackboard and author of “Grokking Software Architecture”, tells host Luca Mezzalira he wrote the book after mentoring junior developers who stared blankly at basic fundamentals, just as AI was raising the bar for entry-level jobs and junior hiring was dropping. His core thesis is that AI only amplifies what you are: it speeds up good developers and accelerates chaos for those without foundations. He argues architects should think of themselves as "clarity engineers", and the book's five-step process reflects that. Start with what you're being asked to build, ask why (the Toyota Five Whys) until you reach the real driver, sketch the design, and write the decision down, including what you are explicitly not optimizing for. There is no perfect solution, only the best one for your constraints (a three-person team with a two-week deadline shouldn't build a web of microservices). Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) keep teams from relitigating the same choice every few weeks, and communication matters because the best idea doesn't always win, the best-communicated one does.

On AI, Erman's warnings are specific. An engineer's value is moving up the chain, from writing code to directing, reviewing, and challenging agents, but skills erode if nobody writes or reads code anymore. The risk isn't that AI writes bad code. It knows every pattern ever created, and without clear constraints it can stitch them into "Frankenstein code" that works today and fails later. "AI told me to" is not a defensible answer in a PR review, and at AI speed you may make four or five architectural decisions in the time you once made one, so planning matters more, not less.
He also explains Hyrum's Law: with enough users, every observable behavior of your API becomes a contract, documented or not. He doesn't expect AI to replace human judgment soon, because much of what matters about a system lives in context nobody has written down. His practical tip for newer developers is to always ask the AI for an adversarial, architect-level review of its own work. His advice for the next six months: step back and gain clarity before you write code (even a "favorites" button hides architectural decisions), and build things to last by separating concerns and keeping them modular. Luca adds that deterministic tools and probabilistic AI work best together.

Born in Palermo in 1902, Carlo Gambino entered the United States illegally in 1921 and rose through the Brooklyn crime family of Vincent Mangano and Albert Anastasia, growing rich on bootleg alcohol and black-market wartime ration stamps. When Anastasia was shot dead in a Manhattan barbershop in October 1957, a murder Gambino is widely believed to have arranged, he took over the family and gave it his name. Softly spoken and careful, he survived the Apalachin raid, years of FBI surveillance and a deportation order, often pleading heart trouble, and died at home in 1976 after naming Paul Castellano as his successor.

items.title: North Korea's alliance with China and Russia | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>For decades, people have predicted the collapse of North Korea. Yet the Kim dynasty seems more entrenched than ever. Propaganda, military posturing and a nuclear program are shoring up Kim Jong Un's power, both domestically and internationally.

This documentary traces North Korea's evolution from an isolated hereditary dictatorship to a state whose nuclear weapons program is cause for global concern. Today, the regime possesses missiles capable of potentially reaching long-range targets. Meanwhile, it is also seeking closer ties with key partners China and Russia. And for the first time, North Korea is deploying thousands of soldiers to fight alongside Russia in its war in Ukraine — a conspicuous move that provides the country combat experience, foreign currency, and access to new military technology.
Drawing on new archival sources, exclusive analysis from experts and insights into North Korea's elaborate propaganda machine, this documentary shows how the regime fosters loyalty and cements its power. A cult of personality, shows of military strength and foreign policy successes all serve to maintain its power at home.
This underscores why Kim Jong Un currently sees himself in a strategically advantageous position — and why Pyongyang's role on the international stage is becoming increasingly significant.
Despite being a small, largely isolated country, North Korea regularly finds itself at the center of geopolitical tensions. Three generations of the Kim dynasty have created a system of government based on control, isolation and military strength. What strategies have allowed the Kim family to continue ruling to this day — and what are the consequences for the region and the world?

items.title: NATO's Plan If Russia Attacks Tomorrow
items.author: fern
items.content:
<article>Taking care of your health just got easier. Spend less time searching and head to https://zocdoc.com/fern to book your next appointment (ad)

Join our newsletter: https://roots.watchfern.com/


What would happen if Russia attacked NATO? Drawing on military wargames, NATO assessments and expert analyses, we play out a hypothetical scenario based on a very real threat: a Russian invasion of the Baltics. How would NATO respond, and why would so much depend on Germany?

Special thanks to Ben Hodges, retired Commanding General of U.S. Army Europe, for the interview. Thank you Dr. Florian Keisinger (ZDS), Lukas Iffländer (ProBahn), retired Generalleutnant Alfons Mais and Jannik Hartmann (NATO Defence College) for sharing their valuable insights and expertise.

Corrections:
00:01 The US intelligence reports describe a possible limited test of NATO in the coming years, from a cyberattack to a small incursion. A land incursion is rated unlikely. The Baltic invasion scenario is based on separate sources.
00:26 Canada should also have been marked on the map as a NATO member.
02:00 The RAND wargames we cite date from 2014–15 and don't reflect Russia's losses in Ukraine or NATO's current presence in the Baltics.
02:50  Building an invasion force while fighting in Ukraine would likely take months and be visible to NATO, giving it time to reinforce.
04:43 The US Army also keeps prepositioned equipment in Europe (APS-2), so reinforcement would be faster than shown.
05:25 Many of Russia's 64 submarines protect its nuclear deterrent. Only a fraction are modern attack submarines, and not all are available at once.
07:30 Kosovo is an independent country, not part of Serbia as wrongly shown in our map.
08:25 “Sukhoi” is the English spelling of the manufacturer, we used the German one “Suchoi”.
14:10 NATO would likely strike Russian supply lines, airfields and Kaliningrad early on, which the scenario doesn't show.

Thanks to Ryan McBeth for his feedback.

items.title: Elite universities are losing Black students
items.author: Vox
items.content:
<article>HBCUs are having a moment.

Many historically Black colleges and universities have seen record-breaking enrollment numbers in their recent freshman classes. But on the flip side of that surge, Black freshman enrollment is actually down by 27 percent among the top 50 most selective institutions in the United States. And there are some big explanations behind these shifts.

As the landscape of higher education has evolved from the eras of segregation to the civil rights movement to Trump-era racial politics, Black students have had to adapt on college campuses nationwide as government mandates, school policies, and the dismantling of affirmative action have impacted their education over the years. 

Hosted by Kahlil Greene, this video is part of our new series Kahlil Explains that unites Vox’s unique brand of explainer journalism with Greene’s expertise in how politics and culture shape society. This first episode traces the history of HBCUs and the experience of Black college students to unpack why Black student enrollment is growing at HBCUs yet declining at other elite institutions.

items.title: Inside Major Corporate Accounting Scandals | Bigger Than Enron (full documentary) | FRONTLINE (PBS)
items.author: FRONTLINE PBS | Official
items.content:
<article>Enron’s spectacular collapse in the early 2000s was at the time the biggest financial scandal in U.S. history. It didn’t happen in a vacuum — and it revealed systemic problems far beyond a single company. (Aired 2002)

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb

And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate

In the 2002 documentary “Bigger Than Enron,” Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist Hedrick Smith looked at Enron’s implosion and asked, “Where were the watchdogs who were supposed to warn us when companies were playing fast and loose with their books — the stock analysts, lawyers, bankers, Securities and Exchange Commission? Above all, where were the accountants?”

“Bigger Than Enron” investigated those questions in detail, offering an in-depth look at where the U.S. financial regulation landscape stood in June 2002 after Enron’s collapse. 
The documentary is now streaming on YouTube for the first time as part of an effort to make FRONTLINE’s multi-decade reporting archive widely accessible.  

In the film, experts told Smith that what happened at Enron — a cozy collaboration between the company and its accounting firm, Arthur Andersen, that enabled Enron to overstate its profits — was far from anomalous. Smith reported that in what was described as the “go-go ‘90s,” the drive for profits was in full swing, and big accounting firms regularly worked hand-in-glove with clients and Wall Street to find loopholes in accounting rules that made companies look more successful than they really were.

“This is day-to-day business operations in accounting firms and on Wall Street,” Lynn Turner, a former Wall Street partner at an accounting firm before becoming the SEC's chief accountant, said of such practices at the time. “There is nothing extraordinary, nothing unusual in that respect, with respect to Enron.”

“Bigger Than Enron” examined three specific cases involving Andersen where misleading or fraudulent accounting practices caused enormous investor losses — at Sunbeam, Waste Management, and finally, Enron — and explored the downfall of Andersen, a firm that had previously built its reputation on rock-ribbed integrity.

The documentary also looked at how, in the decade leading up to Enron, accounting and financial industry lobbyists had successfully flexed their muscle on Capitol Hill in three battles: the fight over tort reform, the fight over stock options, and the war over a SEC attempt to rein in conflicts of interest by forcing accounting firms to separate their auditing and consulting practices.

Visit pbs.org/frontline to read about legal and regulatory developments since this documentary aired, including the Supreme Court’s 2005 overturning of Arthur Andersen’s obstruction of justice conviction.

“Bigger Than Enron” was a FRONTLINE coproduction with Hedrick Smith Productions. The writer, producer and director was Marc Shaffer. The producer and correspondent was Hedrick Smith. The executive editor of FRONTLINE was Louis Wiley Jr. The executive producer of FRONTLINE was David Fanning.

items.title: Inside ICE: The fight against Trump's deportations | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Donald Trump's immigration crackdown is facing resistance across the United States. And not just from migrants. Local residents are fighting back, determined to stop new ICE detention centers from being built in their own backyards.

Rodney Taylor was just two years old when he arrived in the US from Liberia on a medical visa. By the age of 10, both his legs had been amputated. Georgia became his home, where he raised a family and worked as a barber. But his immigration status remained unresolved.
In early 2025, Rodney was arrested by officers from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The arrest was based on a burglary conviction from his youth. The state of Georgia had already pardoned him for that offence in 2010.
Rodney spent 15 months behind bars at the Stewart Detention Center in southern Georgia. Today, he's back with his family. But he faces deportation. And his future in the country he has called home for almost his entire life hangs in the balance.
Meanwhile, some 200 kilometers (125 miles) north, the Trump administration was planning a massive new ICE detention center to hold up to 10,000 people. But in Social Circle, a small town in the heart of Trump country, the plans sparked an unexpected backlash. A progressive activist and a Trump supporter found themselves on the same side of a political battle, united by one goal: to stop the detention center from being built.

items.title: The Most Profitable Subway on Earth
items.author: Bloomberg Originals
items.content:
<article>Hong Kong’s Mass Transit Railway is the most profitable transit system in the world. While subways tend to lose money everywhere else, the MTR funds its system through a real estate engine known as “land-value capture.” By directly integrating malls, offices and apartments into stations, the railway has created a self-funding loop that pays billions of dollars back to the government.

Now, the MTR is taking on a massive challenge: funding transport for the Northern Metropolis, a new tech hub aimed at better connecting Hong Kong with Mainland China. But as local real estate cools, construction costs soar and residents shift retail spending across the border to Shenzhen, the MTR is taking on record debt to fund the expansion. Will this ambitious project break the very rule that made Hong Kong’s transit a global marvel?

items.title: Greece's mobile hospital: Providing medical care to remote islands | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Greece has more than 200 inhabited islands, many of which lack medical facilities. Fortunately, there are doctors who travel to even the most remote Aegean islands, providing health care on a volunteer basis.

This film follows a group of health workers as they travel to the island of Serifos. With two trucks full of medical equipment, they set up a temporary hospital there, which will operate for several days.

Ten years ago, Greece's Stavros Niarchos Foundation established a system of mobile medical teams. Each month, they travel by ferry from Athens to provide medical care to small, remote islands for short periods. Many islanders cannot afford the cost of a visit to a doctor on the mainland, and in winter, sea crossings are often impossible due to bad weather.

Ophthalmologist Christos Christoulakis has been involved from the very beginning: "We give something, but we also get so much in return," he says. He's on his way to Serifos together with Tasos Stamatiadis, the mission's technical director. The ferry is also carrying two trucks of medical equipment, including a portable X-ray machine, a 3D mammography machine, and a bone density scanner. In just a few hours, a pop-up hospital will be set up on Serifos, and for a few days the island will have the medical infrastructure of a small town. There are also many other specialists and nurses, all working on a volunteer basis. The island's residents eagerly await the medical team. Many of the population of nearly 1,500 get checkups, often seeing several different specialists. Crucially, the "traveling hospital" allows people to continue living on Serifos despite the lack of infrastructure. However, some patients are advised to seek treatment on the mainland — such as Susanna Diogou, who is experiencing the symptoms of paralysis in her left foot. But leaving to get medical care also means being separated from her family for an extended period — a dilemma faced by many people on Greece's remote islands.

A former schoolteacher from the Texas Hill Country, Lyndon Baines Johnson rose through Congress to become Senate majority leader and then John F. Kennedy's vice president. Sworn in aboard Air Force One after Kennedy's assassination in Dallas in November 1963, he pushed through the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, beat Barry Goldwater in a landslide and launched the Great Society, including Medicare and Medicaid. At the same time the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution opened the way to a vast escalation of the war in Vietnam, and in March 1968 he announced that he would not seek re-election.

items.title: Only kings could afford that dish in 1300
items.author: French Cooking Academy
items.content:
<article>Long before roux, butter-heavy pan sauces, and haute cuisine, how did royal cooks prepare a feast in medieval France? In this episode, we step back into the 14th century to cookbook called le Viandier by Guillaume Tirel (known as Taillevent) one of the earliest and most famous medieval culinary manuscripts.

We are making a historic Civet de Porc (spiced pork stew). This recipe reveals forgotten medieval techniques: pre-roasting the meat to mimic open spit-roasting, thickening the rich braising liquid entirely with toasted bread soaked in wine and broth, and finishing the sauce with an aromatic blend of prized medieval spices, including Java long pepper, cinnamon, ginger, and saffron. Spices back then were so expensive that only kings could afford them.

Full recipe: https://www.thefrenchcookingacademy.com/recipes/medieval-pork-stew

Ingredients & Measurements

The Pork & Base:

1 kg (2.2 lbs) Pork shoulder or pork scotch, cut into stewing cubes
2 large brown onions, sliced
1 tbsp cooking fat (rendered pork lard or oil)
3 slices rustic sourdough or country bread, heavily toasted
300 ml dry light red wine like pinot or gamay
600 ml rich meat stock or broth (to cover)
Salt to taste
The Medieval Spice Blend & Finish:

2 tsp Java long pepper (or freshly ground black pepper)
2 tsp ground cinnamon
1 tsp ground ginger
A generous pinch of saffron threads, chopped
2 tbsp verjuice (or white wine vinegar / cider vinegar)
3 tbsp aged red wine vinegar

items.title: Can Trump steal the midterms? | America, Actually

items.content:
<article>Between the Trump administration’s executive orders, lawsuits, and relentless rhetoric, it can feel as though America’s voting systems are under constant threat. Just this week, President Trump said he asked the Justice Department to sue Alaska to block certification of the state’s Senate race if the Republican candidate loses. But beyond these headlines, what’s actually happening to your vote?

This week on America, Actually, Vox’s Astead Herndon sits down with Eliza Sweren-Becker, the deputy director of the Voting Rights and Elections Program at the Brennan Center for Justice, for a reality check on election security. Despite high-profile threats, Donald Trump is currently on a losing streak in court, and election advocates are racking up major wins.

items.title: The Navy’s Secret Plan For World War III
items.author: Mustard
items.content:
<article>Get Nebula for 50% off using my link: https://go.nebula.tv/mustard 

Watch Unsealed Episode 3 here: https://nebula.tv/videos/mustard-the-insane-plan-to-land-airliners-on-aircraft-carriers

In the mid-1950s, as the Cold War intensified, the Soviet Union tested its first true hydrogen bomb, raising the terrifying prospect of a nuclear attack on American soil. The United States had a dangerous weakness: its nuclear bombers sat on predictable airfields, vulnerable to a surprise Soviet strike. If many of America’s bombers were destroyed before they could take off, America could lose its ability to strike back. With its deterrent at risk, the Cold War had entered a dangerous new phase. 

The Navy had an audacious solution: a jet-powered flying boat that could deliver a nuclear strike without ever needing a runway. The Martin P6M SeaMaster would be the centerpiece of what the Navy called the Seaplane Striking Force, a fleet of bombers that would lie in wait, take off from the ocean at a moment’s notice, fly low to evade enemy radar, and strike Soviet targets from the sea. When the order came, these bombers could strike before the Soviets knew it was coming.

But there was a problem. The Navy wasn’t supposed to have its own nuclear bomber fleet. Strategic bombing belonged to the Air Force. Instead, the Navy officially presented the SeaMaster as a high-speed minelayer. Behind the cover story, engineers were working tirelessly to turn an enormous seaplane into a near-supersonic strike aircraft that would rival the Air Force’s B-52. It meant battling punishing ocean conditions, violent vibrations, and a series of dangerous setbacks.

By 1959, the redesigned SeaMaster was closer than ever to becoming operational. But a new threat emerged, and it didn’t come from the Soviet Union.</article>

items.title: Between the czar and Hitler - The forgotten story of the White Army | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>The Russian Civil War was one of the 20th century's bloodiest chapters. The fight for Russia between Lenin's Red Army and the White Army was ruthless. Its legacy can be felt in Europe to this day.

Nestled in the Alps in Austrian East Tyrol, a cemetery bears witness to a dark chapter in European history. In 1945, following 27 years of war, flight and survival, the White Army's long journey came to a tragic end there.

Russia, 1917: Czar Nicholas II was forced to abdicate, bringing 300 years of Romanov rule to an end. Lenin and his wife, Nadezhda Krupskaya, returned from exile in Switzerland determined to reshape the country according to their vision. But alongside the Bolsheviks, Lenin's radical communist followers, another force emerged to claim Russia: The White Army.

The White Army was made up largely of generals and officers from the former czarist armed forces, who openly opposed the Communists. Women were also among its ranks — including Maria Bochkareva, who commanded the famous Women's Battalion of the White Army. Until 1922, the Red and White armies waged a brutal struggle for the control of Russia.

After its defeat, the White Army fled to the Balkans, while many other supporters of the czar scattered across Europe. Paris filled with Russians driven into exile. Former princesses often made their living as art models — they saw no future in a country ruled by the Red Army.

When Hitler invaded the Soviet Union, former White Army soldiers saw another chance to fight the hated Bolsheviks. Many openly sympathized with Nazi Germany, viewing it as a defense against Stalin.

By the end of World War II, the White Army was left confronting its own ruined hopes for a Russia liberated from Bolshevik rule.

This documentary traces the history of the White Army and explores a little-known chapter of European history — one that spans revolution, exile and political radicalization.

items.title: Can Japan’s Economy Afford Takaichi’s Big Bet?
items.author: Bloomberg Originals
items.content:
<article>A year after becoming Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi is pursuing an ambitious plan to build a stronger, richer and more secure country. At the center of her strategy is a target of ¥370 trillion ($2.3 trillion) in public and private investment, spanning artificial intelligence, semiconductors, defense, energy, food technology and even manga.

But as Takaichi enters her second year in power, Japan faces a formidable combination of pressures: a weak yen, rising living costs, a shrinking workforce, enormous government debt and worsening relations with China. Takaichi also wants Japan to spend more on defense as security challenges grow across Asia.

This documentary examines Takaichi’s first year as prime minister, the forces that brought her to power and the risks surrounding her agenda.

items.content:
<article>This presentation was recorded at Bug Bash EU 2026.
https://antithesis.com/bugbash/europe/2026/

Anatoliy Bilenko - Staff Engineer at Canonical
Alberto Carretero - Software Engineer at Canonical

ORIGINAL TALK TITLE
Building a Reliable Database Protocol with AI, Formal Methods, and a
Simulation Framework

RESOURCES
Anatoliy
https://www.linkedin.com/in/anatoliy-bilenko

Alberto
https://www.linkedin.com/in/angel-alberto-carretero

ABSTRACT
Building a critical distributed protocol in 2026 means treating correctness as a continuous engineering practice, not a final verification step.

This talk presents a workflow that combines executable state-machine designs and formal methods with AI-assisted development, observability, and Antithesis testing.

The goal is to move from a protocol model to evidence from real-system executions: expose meaningful events, generate and investigate failure scenarios, and use code together with observability data to validate distributed properties that code alone cannot reveal. [...]

In Frankfurt, Hatice Nizam runs two exclusive hair salons under the name "HaarWerk," serving clients from all over the world. She's spent three decades in the industry and has long been a star on social media, where she's known as the "Queen of Blonde Shades."

Dr. Tamarica Fischer-Nagel is a cosmetic surgeon. Together with her partner, Dr. Patrice Moubayed, she runs practices in Bad Wildungen and Kassel in central Germany. items.title: The Secret Rearmament of the Weimar Republic, 1919–1933
items.author: Sir Manatee
items.content:
<article>If you like my videos and want to support me, then you can do that here:  https://www.patreon.com/c/SirManateee

Thank you :) 

Tips: https://ko-fi.com/sirmanatee

Thumbnail design by: Borys Vision [https://www.behance.net/basvision]

During the November Revolution of 1918, the German military had been virtually disempowered: A democratic government had taken over in the country, people were angry at the army for failing to win WW1 and for ruling Germany with an iron fist and the workers' and soldiers' councils renounced the power of command from their officers. But after just a couple of months, the military was back in power and what's more is that it immediately set about rearming the country. But how did the Weimar Republic even secretly rearm in the first place? How much did the government know about this? And in what ways did it pave the way for the rearmament of the Wehrmacht after 1933? Watch the video to find out!

items.title: Open Source Is Under Attack & AI Made It Worse • Steve Poole & Olimpiu Pop • GOTO 2026
items.author: GOTO Conferences
items.content:
<article>This interview was recorded for GOTO Unscripted. #GOTOcon #GOTOunscripted
https://gotopia.tech

Steve Poole - Developer Advocate at HeroDevs & Community Director at London Java Community
Olimpiu Pop - Technologist & Tech Journalist

Check out more here:
https://gotopia.tech/articles/457

RESOURCES
Steve
https://x.com/spoole167
https://github.com/spoole167
https://www.linkedin.com/in/noregressions

Olimpiu
https://x.com/olimpiupop
https://github.com/zroll
https://www.linkedin.com/in/olimpiupop

DESCRIPTION
Steve Poole of HeroDevs, a longtime voice on software supply chain security, tells host Olimpiu Pop that the landscape has hit a "watershed moment" in the last few weeks. The long-standing attack methods are simple: typo'd or confusingly named packages, unchecked scripts, inflated version numbers that trick builds into pulling the wrong release, and maintainers who build trust and then turn bad. Developers are among the weakest links because their machines hold so many credentials. The new factor is AI-driven vulnerability discovery, which both attackers and security researchers are using. Steve's concern is that discovery is now industrialized while fixing is not: maintainers who once saw a CVE or two a year may now face batches of them, and he fears more will simply walk away. Unsupported packages are especially exposed, since CVEs against them often never get reported at all. His worst-case scenario is that open source security fixes end up arriving in small commercial enclaves first, as regulation and cyber insurers push companies to pay for maintenance.

The practical advice for engineers is concrete. Fixing an open source dependency yourself is fine once, but then CVEs two through six arrive and you are in the maintenance business. Instead, scrutinize and reduce your dependencies, noting that studies suggest AI-generated apps pick roughly three times more of them than people do. Stay as close to HEAD as you can on maintained releases, and build your pipelines into "sleek engines" that can upgrade continuously, because under the EU Cyber Resilience Act "best efforts" to fix a vulnerability will not mean a migration in six months (Steve is clear he is not a lawyer). The two close on responsibility: like a compiler's output, AI-generated code is still your code, as Kubernetes' AI policy makes explicit by ruling out AI co-authorship. The hard part is the non-deterministic output, which means thinking harder about testing and proving quality. Steve's closing hope is that the industry becomes more pragmatic about AI's downsides, though he admits so many forces are converging that it's hard to predict where this ends.

items.title: What Is Hiding in the Milky Way's Core?
items.author: Astrum
items.content:
<article>This one image is starting an exoplanet revolution. JMP is an interactive statistical discovery software for scientists and engineers to explore data visually, uncover meaningful patterns, and make confident data-driven decisions. Check out http://jmp.com/astrum for your free trial.

▀▀▀▀▀▀

On 23rd March 2025 the Euclid telescope captured the most detailed visible-light image ever taken of the cosmic bulge of our Milky Way galaxy. It’s packed with 60 million stars, but that’s not all. And where there are stars, there are planets - millions of them. Could this image be the key to finding them?

items.title: Killing time - The science of boredom | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Our modern lives are wired for productivity, speed and constant stimulation. Boredom? No time! Yet boredom can fire up our creativity and help teach us to manage our emotions.

In a world built for productivity, speed and nonstop stimulation, it seems there's little room left for boredom. Smartphones offer us endless distraction, making it easy to avoid the uncomfortable feeling. But what actually is boredom? And why do we feel it? Everybody experiences boredom, yet few of us take it seriously. Researchers around the world are working to better understand it — because beneath that nagging sense of emptiness lies far more than most people realize.

The documentary is an entertaining exploration of how boredom can be not only unpleasant — but also beneficial. Feeling bored encourages us to look for ways out of dull situations and can help boost our creativity. It also plays an important role in childhood, as we learn to manage our emotions. Researchers do caution against idealizing boredom, though. When it becomes chronic, it can contribute to problems such as alcoholism, and internet and gambling addictions.

We all know boredom — yet we all experience it differently. Is it an agonizing emptiness, or a driving force behind creativity? Nervous restlessness, or restful calm? In fascinating experiments, researchers in psychology, neuroscience and philosophy explore this elusive feeling. How can some people tolerate boredom better than others? How much boredom is healthy — and what actually happens in the brain when nothing is happening? Spoiler: Quite a lot!

Today's complex software is open: trusted internal code is tightly intertwined with untrusted external code whose behaviour may be unknown, or even adversarial. items.title: What TPS’ End Means for Haitians | Haiti Deportation Crisis (full documentary) | FRONTLINE (PBS)
items.author: FRONTLINE PBS | Official
items.content:
<article>The Trump administration ended Temporary Protected Status for hundreds of thousands of Haitians who had fled violence and upheaval, saying that Haiti was now safe enough for them to return home. What is the reality on the ground in Haiti?

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb

And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate

“Haiti Deportation Crisis” offers a rare, up-close look at the extent and impact of gang violence in Haiti, the efforts to combat it, and the rising fears among Haitians in the U.S. of being sent back.
  
In vivid detail, the documentary shows how armed gangs now control large parts of Haiti, how massacres and mass kidnappings are devastating families, and how efforts to stem the violence are playing out so far — including the work of the Gang Suppression Force, a newly-established international military mission backed by the U.N. and 18 countries including the U.S.

Unfolding against the backdrop of the end of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haitians, what emerges is a visceral documentation of life inside a country many Haitians in the U.S. say is as dangerous as ever  — and where they fear they’ll be kidnapped, ransomed, or killed if they’re deported. The documentary also examines how the end of TPS is impacting communities in the U.S. with large Haitian populations, such as Springfield, Ohio.

items.title: In the shadow of copper - The price of mining in Serbia | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>The small Serbian town of Bor lives from copper mining. Many residents say that high levels of pollution from the mine, which has been majority-owned by a Chinese corporation since 2018, are making them sick.

Resistance is growing in the town Bor in eastern Serbian. Lazar Milutinovic and Marko Andrejevic are members of the student movement that has been driving social change in Serbia for more than two years. Meanwhile, others point to the high levels of heavy metal contamination measured in the area, the high incidence of cancer and the low life expectancy.

Environmental engineer Snezana Serbula has spent her entire professional career investigating the mine’s impact on Bor. One of Serbia’s most prominent critics of mining, she has published numerous scientific studies on the effects of heavy metal emissions on the environment and on human health.

In this report, workers say they were not adequately informed about the possible long-term consequences of mining. Meanwhile, local residents accuse the authorities and the company of a lack of transparency. Lazar and Marko have founded an opposition movement in the town, calling for greater oversight and stricter environmental regulations.

Jasna Tomic lives in the village of Krivelj near Bor. She could soon lose her home: The village, which has been inhabited by the Vlach ethnic minority for centuries, is expected to make way for the mine. Many of her neighbors have already left. Jasna fears she, too, will soon have to relocate. She is fighting to ensure that the village community can at least find a new home together.

A Film by Eberhard Rühle, Nikolaus Tarouquella and Natalija Miletić

DESCRIPTION
Rebecca Le and Zach Daniel, co-authors of "Ash Framework: Create Declarative Elixir Web Apps" and maintainers of the framework, tell host Christian Alexander how the book came to be: Rebecca wanted to write the guide she wished she'd had when learning Ash, where all the pieces existed but it wasn't clear how they fit together. The book builds a music-database app (Tunez) in small steps and adds authentication, policies, and testing at the point a real project would need them, rather than front-loading the hardest material. The surprising conclusion is that writing it changed the framework. Ash had deliberately offered no testing guidance, but when Zach tried to explain how to test, he found it couldn't be explained as things stood, so they built the generator-based testing support that now ships with Ash. Zach also describes the framework's core bet as extensibility: where Rails is "omakase," Ash is a Chipotle bowl, with extensions (event sourcing, TypeScript bindings, Ash AI) that can reshape how everything works, which is why the book's foundational concepts have stayed stable even as the ecosystem moved quickly.

For engineers weighing a framework, the discussion offers a few concrete takeaways. Ash's learning curve is steep up front but flattens: once you know resources, actions, and policies, hard problems like APIs, authentication internals, and nested forms reuse the same concepts. Zach recalls a client whose API layer ended up as a single line of code, though he's candid that a line that powerful has to be understood (hence his lightsaber analogy). Rebecca built the first version of the Cinder data table library in about a week, and Zach's team at Remedy replaced a half-baked in-house version with it and deleted a large amount of code. Finally, Zach reports that AI has made the up-front cost much easier to absorb: at his company, engineers who had never learned Elixir are delivering on an Ash project in under three weeks, and basic "I got this error" questions have nearly disappeared from the community Discord.

items.title: One electric truck's road trip to Norway | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Trucker Tobias Wagner's mission: to get from Germany's East Frisia to Norway in an electric truck. A navigation buoy from the Juister Riff in the North Sea went missing and has turned up in Scandinavia. Now, it's Wagner's job to bring it back.

Tackling 900 kilometers, three countries and a ferry crossing — all in an electric truck. To make the trip work, Wagner has had to plan his route carefully. Weight, distance and road incline all affect the truck's range. Finding suitable overnight stops is also crucial, since not all truck parking areas have charging stations.

Many in his industry are still skeptical about electric trucks. But freight hauler Nanno Janssen has no doubt: e-trucks are the future. Sixty percent of his fleet already runs on electricity, and he plans to transition the remaining trucks in the coming years. Tobias Wagner is a believer, too. He regularly shares his experiences as "Elektrotrucker" on YouTube.

The film follows Wagner on this unusual assignment. It shows how today's electric mobility is already working for long-haul trucking — and looks at the challenges that remain.

items.title: The Horrifying Truth About Willowbrook State School
items.author: Weird History
items.content:
<article>In 1942, New York opened the Willowbrook State School on Staten Island, promising care and support for people with developmental disabilities. But behind its doors, a shocking nightmare unfolded, one that would expose horrifying conditions, abuse, neglect, and a system that failed the very people it was meant to protect.

On this episode of Weird History we take a look at what really happened inside Willowbrook, the investigative reporting that exposed its shocking reality, and the events that helped change the way people with disabilities were treated. How did conditions become so horrific in the first place? And what finally forced the institution to close?
